rv.q: It is a vision of love, guttering in the void; a strange dream of America, falling through the night.
I loathe The Glass Menagerie — and did so the first time I saw it as a teenager — yet this is a strong rendition of the play, should your taste run to claustrophobic glumness.

Sadly, even she couldn’t make me fall for Jeremy Herrin’s underwhelming production of The Glass Menagerie. Tennessee Williams’ breakthrough 1944 play is full of moving autobiographical details, as a man, Tom, recalls his stifled St Louis upbringing with his overbearing mother and excruciatingly shy sister.
This production dials up the fondness for her old-worldly character: her querulously thin voice works, with just how still everything else is. More force would overwhelm things.
This long scene is worth the price of admission alone as Brian J Smith and Kate O'Flynn convey an aching tenderness and mutual generosity that only makes the conclusion more poignant.
Nevertheless, the pain and the humour of Williams’s writing shine through by dint of three splendid performances.

cn.t: Cherry Jones delivers a formidable performance as the domineering southern belle Amanda in this acclaimed revival of Tennessee Williams's breakthrough memory play, with critics praising the production's authenticity and emotional power.
